To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the probability of self competition (and the probability of meeting one's own genes) is higher in communities with high clonality and low diversity, and that community fitness can be expressed as a product of the two variables, anti-diversity and the degree of sexuality.

(a) the probability of wasteful self-competition increases with the degree of clonality in the community and with the decrease of diversity; (b) community fitness is the product of two factors, one being the degree of sexuality and the other the anti-diversity; and (c) the probability of self competition is a key factor in the selection of sexuality versus non-sexuality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the forces that have shaped the evolution of plant community diversity and the forces that have governed the selection among different reproductive modes in plant communities.
the factors that determine the relative abundance of sexual and non-sexual species at community level.
the forces that govern the selection of sexuality versus clonality at community level.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the context of plant communities, sexuality is the more progressive trait, but clonality is the more advantageous one.
the probability of self competition is the key factor in the evolution of clonality and sexuality at community level.

the selection of clonality versus sexual reproduction in plant communities has been influenced by two main factors, the probability of meeting own genes for wastful competition, and the average fitness of the community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
clonality and sexuality are two sides of the same coin.
, the higher the anti-diversity and the lower the degree of sexuality, the higher the community fitness.
clonality has been favored in plant communities where the probability of self competition was high, while sexuality was favored where this probability was low.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the forces that have governed clonality and sexuality in plant communities are likely to be different from those that have influenced the evolution of these life-history traits at population level.
the forces that have shaped community composition have also influenced the evolution of sexual reproduction in plants, and that the forces that govern the two are the same.
the community-level fitness is maximized when the diversity is intermediate, and when the degree of sexuality is also intermediate (i.e., the community is neither too clonal nor too sexual).
